The door opened inward without a sound. Cold water swept across Mara’s shoes, carrying the paper boat between her feet. Beyond the threshold, the little girl lowered her hand.

Tomas caught Mara’s sleeve. “That isn’t you.”

“No,” Mara said. “Not yet.”

The girl smiled, and the chamber’s black water rippled around her ankles. On the far wall, names shone in blue. Hundreds of them, scratched into the stone—some crossed out, some written twice. At the bottom, a fresh line appeared:

TOMAS VALE.

He released Mara. “Close it.”

The watch began to tick backward. With every beat, the water retreated from the chamber, revealing pale shapes beneath its surface: doors, windows, a staircase descending through the floor. The girl’s red scarf fluttered though there was no wind.

“You left me here,” she said.

Mara looked at the watch. Its hands had stopped at the hour her mother disappeared. She had spent years believing the watch had belonged to her mother alone.

“I was six,” Mara whispered.

“And I was waiting.”

Tomas stepped between them. The name on the wall flared brighter, then split down the middle. A crack raced through the chamber, dividing the girl from the door.

The child seized Mara’s wrist. “Choose quickly. The river can take one name back—or carry all of us through.”

Behind them, the passage filled with the sound of distant bells. Tomas looked at the glowing inscription, then at Mara.

She reached for the little girl.
